title: Investment: Sovereign wealth funds bypassing Australia: Macquarie
full_text:
Sovereign wealth funds are avoiding investments in Australia due to punishing approvals processes and long delays to get deals done, Macquarie chief executive Shemara Wikramanayake has warned, adding that the country needs to move faster to streamline regulation.
Urging policymakers to adopt more of a "sense of crisis", Wikramanayake said Australia was at risk of losing out to rivals such as the United States, United Kingdom, Canada and Singapore as they stepped up efforts to attract global capital.
"We have sovereign wealth funds that are saying they either will now not invest in Australia or have a much higher required return because of experiences they've had in terms of delays or unexpected outcomes and lack of certainty," Wikramanayake told an infrastructure summit in Sydney.
She made the comments after a survey from Infrastructure Partnerships Australia this week showed the nation had dropped to second as the most popular place to invest, losing the top spot to the US.
While 56 per cent of investors nominated Australia as a preferred market, unchanged from last year, the US surged from 48 per cent to 80 per cent.
Wikramanayake said the shift was not confined to the US, with European countries also gaining ground and markets such as Hong Kong and Singapore taking an entrepreneurial approach to working with businesses and attracting capital.
Australia needed to remove barriers to new investment and better co-ordinate approvals across government.
She said a telecommunications chief executive told her that laying 1800 kilometres of fibre from Brisbane to Melbourne required 6000 approvals, while the sector faced about 200 legislative and regulatory requirements.
"There's scope for us to do more," she said, noting that foreign investment approval processes were increasingly streamlined in the US, UK, Canada and Singapore.
Although Wikramanayake welcomed the federal government's move towards a risk-based approach to foreign investment approvals, she said uncertainty and delays already influenced how international investors viewed Australia.
She said Australia risked becoming complacent because of its economic stability and quality of life.
"We just need to bring ourselves to a bit more of this sense of crisis at the moment to think medium-term."
Australia needed to create opportunities to put more of its roughly $4.8 trillion pool of retirement savings to work domestically, Wikramanayake said, or risk an acceleration in those funds being deployed in offshore markets.
Australia remained well-positioned thanks to strong institutions and stable government, particularly as global investors shifted more money into private credit and real assets such as infrastructure.
But she said maintaining that advantage would require Australia to respond as competing markets more aggressively courted capital.
Macquarie is preparing for its first leadership transition in almost eight years, with Greg Ward taking over from Wikramanayake in November.
Wikramanayake, who will retire after an almost four-decade career at the investment bank, backed Ward to succeed, pointing to his role building Macquarie's digital bank and experience in navigating shifts in technology, regulation and governance.
Macquarie saw technology as driving the next wave of investment, and Wikramanayake said artificial intelligence was likely to be a bigger enabler than cloud computing was a decade ago, spurring investment beyond data centres into energy, cooling, land, cabling and fibre networks.
Macquarie also expected capital to increasingly flow into energy, defence, supply chains, logistics and critical minerals as governments and companies prioritised making the economy more resilient to external shocks.
